title: Common-Size, Trend & Segment Analysis — Comparing MBG and Riverton Fairly (CMA P2-A · feeds BAR)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — you cannot compare a $12.5M entity to a $16.9M entity by dollars

Fictionalized case facts: the MBG GL totals $12,480,000.00 and Riverton totals $16,920,000.00, and a standing rule is that the two entities are never combined on one statement — each is reported as its own segment. So how do you tell which entity is structurally healthier when one is a third larger? You normalize. Common-size analysis restates every line as a percentage, removing the size effect so structure and trend become comparable across entities and across years.

Vertical (common-size) analysis

Common-size the income statement by dividing every line by revenue, and the balance sheet by dividing every line by total assets. Using week 2's illustrative MBG statements:

Common-size income statement (÷ revenue $24,000,000)

Revenue 100.0%; cost of revenue 86.0%; gross profit 14.0%; general & administrative 7.5%; operating income 6.5%; interest 1.08%; pretax income 5.42%; income tax 1.30%; net income 4.12%. Now a margin problem is visible regardless of revenue size — a contractor whose cost of revenue runs 90% has a 10% gross margin no matter how big the top line is.

Common-size balance sheet (÷ total assets $12,000,000)

Current assets 50.0%; net property & equipment 41.7%; other 8.3%; current liabilities 25.0%; long-term debt & other 40.0%; total liabilities 65.0%; equity 35.0%. The 65% liability share is the same story as week 1's debt-to-assets of 0.65 — common-size and ratios are two views of the same structure.

Horizontal (trend) analysis

Horizontal analysis compares the same line across periods. Assume an illustrative prior year with revenue $21,000,000 and net income $760,000.

Revenue growth = ($24,000,000 − $21,000,000) ÷ $21,000,000 = 14.3%. Expressed as a trend index with the prior year = 100, current revenue indexes to ($24,000,000 ÷ $21,000,000) × 100 = 114.3.

Net income growth = ($988,000 − $760,000) ÷ $760,000 = 30.0%. Net income grew far faster than revenue (30.0% vs 14.3%), which means the net margin expanded — from $760,000 ÷ $21,000,000 = 3.62% last year to 4.12% this year. Trend plus common-size together tell you not just that profit rose, but that it rose because of margin, not just volume.

Segment comparison — MBG vs Riverton

Because the entities are reported separately (a real consolidation rule — never combine MBG and Riverton), common-size is the honest way to compare them. Suppose Riverton's common-size cost of revenue is 88.0% versus MBG's 86.0%. Riverton is the larger entity by GL dollars ($14.03M vs $10.60M) yet converts a smaller share of each revenue dollar into gross profit. Size hid that; common-size reveals it. The same approach compares either entity to industry benchmarks, since published construction benchmarks are expressed as percentages.

Segment reporting discipline matters: combining the two would overstate scale and mask that the structural margin difference lives in one entity. The intercompany balances between them (covered next week) must be eliminated before any consolidated view — but for performance comparison, you keep them separate and common-size each.

Market ratios and the private-company limit

Market-based ratios extend analysis to share value: earnings per share = net income ÷ weighted-average shares; price/earnings = market price per share ÷ EPS; dividend yield = dividends per share ÷ market price. These require a traded price. MBG is privately held, so there is no market price and P/E cannot be computed directly. Analysts instead apply comparable public-company multiples or precedent-transaction multiples to MBG's earnings to estimate value. Recognizing this limit is itself an exam point: do not report a market ratio for an entity that has no market price.

Combining the two lenses — and the benchmarks that matter

Vertical and horizontal analysis are most powerful together. A common-size statement tells you the structure in one period; a trend index tells you the direction; reading both at once isolates the cause of a change. Suppose MBG's cost of revenue rose from 84.0% to 86.0% of revenue (vertical) while revenue grew 14.3% (horizontal). The combined read is unambiguous: the business got bigger but less efficient per dollar — volume up, margin compressed — which is a very different story from a contractor whose margin held as it grew. On the income statement, the gross-profit line is the one to watch in construction; on the balance sheet, the current-liability and equity percentages reveal the leverage structure that month one's debt-to-assets ratio measured directly.

Choosing benchmarks. A common-size or trend figure is meaningless in isolation; it needs a comparator. The three standard references are the entity's own history (is the structure drifting?), close peers, and published industry data — for construction, sources such as surety and contractor financial surveys that report median percentages by revenue band. Because those benchmarks are expressed as percentages, common-size is the only way to line MBG, Riverton, and an industry median up on the same axis. The size gap that made the raw GL totals ($12.5M vs $16.9M) incomparable disappears once every line is a share of its own base.

Pitfalls in common-size and trend work

Several traps recur. First, a small or volatile base distorts a trend index — a line that grows from $2,000 to $4,000 shows a 100% jump that means little in dollars. Second, changing the denominator mid-comparison (revenue redefined, a segment reclassified) silently breaks the trend, the same reprocessing risk the CMA program flagged when a crosswalk version changed. Third, reading a percentage shift without the dollar context: a 1-point rise in cost of revenue on $24,000,000 of revenue is $240,000 of lost gross profit — material to a contractor's thin margin even though "one point" sounds trivial. Always carry the percentage back to dollars before concluding.

What common-size cannot tell you

Normalizing is powerful but it discards one thing on purpose: absolute scale. Two contractors can show nearly identical common-size statements while one is ten times the size of the other — with very different access to bonding, financing, skilled crews, and economies of scale. Percentages can also mask a shrinking business: a firm in decline may hold a stable common-size profile while its dollars steadily erode, which is exactly why common-size is always paired with horizontal dollar-and-index analysis. And a percentage built on a tiny or negative base — near-zero equity, a loss year — can be mathematically valid yet analytically meaningless. Use common-size to compare structure across entities and time; never let it stand in for the absolute dollars, the trend, and the business context behind them.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR pairs common-size and horizontal analysis with interpretation: identify which line drove a margin change, compute a trend index, and read a common-size statement against a benchmark. Expect a question where revenue and net income grow at different rates and you must conclude whether margins expanded or contracted. The segment-comparison logic — normalize before comparing entities of different size — is squarely BAR territory.

Practice and recap

  1. Common-size the income statement (÷ revenue) and balance sheet (÷ total assets).
  2. Compute horizontal growth rates and a trend index against a base year.
  3. Infer margin expansion or contraction by comparing revenue growth to net-income growth.
  4. Use common-size to compare MBG and Riverton — never by combining them.
  5. Know why a private company has no P/E and what is used instead.

Recap: common-size removes size so structure is comparable; trend analysis shows direction; together they reveal that MBG's net income grew 30.0% on 14.3% revenue growth because the margin expanded. Different-sized entities like MBG and Riverton compare only after normalizing.

questions.q: Why is common-size analysis the right tool to compare MBG ($12.5M) and Riverton ($16.9M)?
choices: It combines them into one statement
It removes the size difference so structure is comparable
questions.explain: Common-size normalizes by a base, so entities of different size can be compared on structure; the two are never combined.
